item.title: Sharing a Workspace
item.description:
Share designs from Workspaces 🔗

Five has been working in the orbital-dev workspace — a development sandbox with a local Kubernetes environment (kind) and LocalStack for AWS service emulation. Rex Park, a developer on the Orbital Labs Development team, needs access so he can deploy the microservices-baseline design and test his service changes without touching staging.

Here is how Five shares the orbital-dev workspace with Rex.

item.title: Promoting a Design from Staging to Prod
item.description:
This guide walks through how Five promotes the prod-deployment-v2 design from the orbital-staging workspace to orbital-production, with Zara Osei (Infrastructure Team Admin) approving the environment assignment.

See Meet Five and the Cast for the full Orbital Labs narrative reference.

Overview 🔗

At Orbital Labs, workspaces mirror the deployment pipeline:

Workspace Environment Teams with Access
orbital-staging staging-aws (EKS + S3 + ElastiCache), staging-azure (AKS + Azure Blob + Azure Service Bus) Infrastructure + Development
orbital-production prod-aws (EKS + RDS + S3 + CloudFront + SQS), prod-gcp (GKE + Cloud SQL + Cloud Storage + Pub/Sub) Infrastructure only

Five has finished validating prod-deployment-v2 in staging. The design deploys an EKS cluster, an RDS PostgreSQL database, an S3 bucket, and a CloudFront distribution — the core of Orbital Labs’ AWS production platform.

item.title: Validating Designs
item.description:
How Validation Works 🔗

Meshery uses static analysis to verify your design. It checks all components within your design and all configured and unconfigured properties of your components against well-defined schemas based on Meshery Models.

This comprehensive validation ensures that:

  1. The design adheres to the expected structure and format.

  2. All components are valid and recognized by Meshery.

  3. There are no missing required configurations.

Performing Validation 🔗

  1. To validate your design, navigate to the Actions button at the top of the Design canvas.

item.title: Dry Running a Design
item.description:
A dry run in Meshery simulates the deployment of your design in the selected target environment without making any actual changes. This step is highly beneficial as it helps identify potential issues before they occur, ensuring a smoother and more reliable deployment process.

Each component in your design is submitted to the Kubernetes API server of every selected cluster as a dry-run request. The API server validates the resource exactly as it would on a real apply - schema, field values, admission - and then discards it. Nothing is created, updated, or persisted, so a dry run is safe to repeat as often as you like.

item.title: Importing a Design
item.description:
Kanvas acts as a powerful bridge, enabling you to import your existing application and infrastructure configurations from a wide variety of standard formats. It transforms these configurations into visual, editable, deployable, and shareable designs. This guide covers how to import designs, the supported formats, and important considerations.

Accessing the Import Functionality 🔗

There are multiple ways to import a design.

You can drag a file from your local computer directly onto the Kanvas canvas to import a design.

item.title: Interpreting Component Badges
item.description:
Ever wondered what those little icons in the corners of your components are? Think of them as your component’s real-time status display. These indicators, called badges, give you at-a-glance information about everything from configuration errors to live performance.

A Tale of Two Modes

A badge’s meaning changes completely depending on your current mode. In Designer, badges help you build a valid blueprint. In Operator, they switch to providing real-time operational data from your live instances.

What Each Corner Means 🔗

While the specific badges change depending on your mode, they all follow a consistent placement philosophy. Badges are organized into four quadrants around a component, with each corner reserved for a specific type of information.

item.title: Undeploying Designs
item.description:
To undeploy the resources

  1. Navigate to the Actions button at the top of the Design canvas.

  2. Click on the Undeploy icon.

item.title: Understanding Tool Modes
item.description:
Kanvas Designer offers three modes: Default, Pencil, and Connector, which behave differently based on the context in which they are used. Understanding these modes is essential for effectively interacting with components and the canvas.

You can switch between mouse modes using hotkeys or tool selection. Here are hotkeys that control your mode:

Hotkeys Description
Temporarily enables the alternative mouse mode (default mode vs pan mode)
Switches to pan mode (hand icon)
Switches to default mode irrespective of which mode you are currently using.

Interacting with Components 🔗

Action Cursor Style Behavior Example
Hover default (arrow) Nothing
Click-and-drag move Moves component in the direction of the mouse
Click default (arrow) Displays component toolbar, resize box, and connection handles
Double-click (component) pointer Opens the component configurator
Double-click (textbox) text Enables text editing inside the component
Right-click default (arrow) Opens the circular component context menu
Click-and-hold crosshair Initiates box selection for selecting multiple components
Scroll wheel default (arrow) Pan up or down
Scroll wheel + CMD/CTRL default (arrow) Zoom in/out
Horizontal scroll wheel default (arrow) Pan left or right

Pencil lines do not connect individual components, but offer annotating capability, allowing you to take notes and draw annotations to enhance your designs.

item.title: Deploying Designs
item.description:
1. To deploy a design, navigate to the Actions button at the top of the Design canvas.

  2. Click on the Deploy icon.

  3. This opens a modal that will take you through all the steps before the final deployment.

  4. Click on Open In Operator to see the pre-filtered view of the deployed resources in the cluster

  5. Click Finish

Deployment Errors 🔗

  1. Missing Namespace: This error occurs when you attempt to create a Kubernetes resource without specifying a namespace. Kubernetes requires that all resources have an associated namespace.

item.title: Publishing to Catalog
item.description:
Publishing a design submits it to the Layer5 Cloud Catalog so others can discover, view, and clone it. In Kanvas Designer, the primary publish action lives in Details, not in the Share modal.

Share controls who can open and edit your working design (Private / Public, invites, Copy Link). Publish moves a design through the catalog publication lifecycle (pending review → published). For the full state machine, roles, and FAQs, see Publishing Designs.

item.title: Reviewing Designs
item.description:
Kanvas’s Designer enables you to place comments “inline” with your infrastructure as code. Use comments to offer feedback to team members, take detailed design notes, capture helpful tips for your team members, and include justification as to your infrastructure and application configuration decisions. Pay it forward to your future self by leaving historical record for reference later.

Your comment may be a request for design review, to offer feedback to peers, or to simply record notes.

item.title: Cloning a Design
item.description:
Steps to cloning a design from Catalog using Kanvas 🔗

  1. Switch to Kanvas Designer mode, if not already in it.
  2. In the left ☰ menu, click New → From a template.
  3. Select a design from the list that appears in the panel.
  4. A modal will pop up requesting you to clone (create a copy of) the design you’ve selected.

This will create a copy of the catalog item to a new design, now owned by you.

item.title: Sharing Designs
item.description:
In Kanvas, you can share your designs with other members of your organization and teams, and you can control access permissions. This page describes the different access types for designs and how to effectively use them.

Sharing requires an account

Anonymous visitors to kanvas.new can create and edit designs without signing in, but sharing a design requires a signed-in account. Choosing Share as an anonymous visitor prompts you to sign in; once you do, share as described below.

Sharing Views

You can share and control access to Views in the same fashion as you do for Designs.

Verify People with Access after sharing

In some earlier cases, the Share modal could report success while the grant or revoke was not applied. If you shared a design or view and collaborators still cannot open it—or someone you removed still has access—open Share on that resource and re-check the People with Access list. Re-add anyone who is missing, remove anyone who should not retain access, and confirm that collaborators can open the resource. Always treat People with Access as the source of truth after every share.

item.title: Deleting a Design
item.description:
Deleting a design removes it permanently. There is no trash, no recycle bin, and no undo: the design record is destroyed, and every workspace it was assigned to loses it at the same time. Before you delete, check that what you actually want is not one of the two softer actions described under Related actions that are not deletion.

Who Can Delete a Design 🔗

Deleting a design requires the Delete a design permission, and beyond that you must own the design. A user who holds the permission but is not the owner is refused - only the design’s owner, or a provider administrator, can delete it.

item.title: Embedding Designs
item.description:
Design Embedding enables you to export a design in a format that can be seamlessly integrated into websites, blogs, or platforms supporting HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This embedded version provides an interactive representation of the design, making it easier to share with infrastructure stakeholders.

Embedding Your Design 🔗

To embed your Kanvas design, follow these steps:

  1. Access Embed Option: Within the Kanvas Designer, select the design you wish to embed. Click on the export icon in the menu for the selected design. The export modal will appear, click on the “Embed” option.

item.title: Working with Canvas Objects
item.description: Everything you place on a Kanvas Designer canvas is an object, and every object answers to the same small set of gestures. You add it, you style it, you copy or clone it, you lock it so nobody nudges it, you resize it, and eventually you delete it. That is true whether the object is an Amazon EKS cluster, a dashed section drawn around a group of services, a textbox holding a caption, or a plain shape used as a legend key.

item.title: Exporting Designs
item.description:
Kanvas lets you export a design in several formats, so you can:

  • keep versioned backups
  • collaborate offline
  • push artifacts to OCI-compatible registries or Helm repositories
  • integrate designs into CI/CD or GitOps pipelines
  • embed interactive diagrams in documentation and blogs

Export in Two Steps 🔗

  1. Open the export menu Within the Kanvas Designer, select the design you wish to export in the design drawer. Click on the export icon in the menu for the selected design.
  2. Pick an export format Choose the option that matches your workflow (see table below).

item.title: Add and Configure Components
item.description:
A component is one piece of infrastructure in a design, and its configuration is what Kanvas applies when you deploy. This guide covers placing components on the canvas, editing their configuration, and moving them around by duplicating, copying, and pasting.

You need a design open in Designer mode. Designer is the only mode that allows authoring.

Add a component 🔗

Kanvas offers several ways to place a component. All of them produce the same result: a component in the design, with its configurator open beside it.

item.title: Build Designs
item.description:
These guides cover the tasks you perform while authoring a design in Designer mode. Each one accomplishes a single task and assumes you know what a design, a component, and a relationship are. If you do not, read Designs and Components and Relationships first.

Authoring happens only in Designer mode. Operator mode shows live cluster state and blocks adding, editing, duplicating, and deleting components.

Goal Guide
Add components, edit their configuration, lock, duplicate, copy, and paste them Add and Configure Components
Connect components and remove connections Create Relationships
Draw, label, and annotate a design with shapes, text, and lines Whiteboard on the Canvas
Keep frequently used models one step away in the dock Pin Models to the Dock
Group components by shared labels Work with Tags

For how Kanvas decides which relationships exist and keeps their configuration in sync, read Policy Evaluation.

item.title: Create Your First Design
item.description:
In this tutorial you build a small web application design in Kanvas Designer: a Deployment that runs the application, a ConfigMap that holds its settings, and a Service that exposes it. You start from an empty canvas, connect the components, and save the result. The saved design is the starting point for Deploy and Observe Your First Design.

Along the way you learn what a design is made of, how relationships express the way components depend on each other, and when and how Kanvas saves your work.

item.title: Designs and Components
item.description: A design is the unit of work in Kanvas. It is a declarative description of infrastructure that you author on a canvas, save as a versioned document, share with others, and deploy to your clusters. Components are the building blocks of a design: some represent real infrastructure that Kanvas deploys, and others are annotations that only explain the design. Knowing which is which, and how a design behaves when you save, share, and deploy it, tells you exactly what Kanvas will do with your work.

item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
Kanvas turns cloud native infrastructure into a design you can see, check, and deploy. This section takes you from an empty canvas to resources running in a Kubernetes cluster. Along the way you learn the four ideas that every other Kanvas page builds on, and which parts of Kanvas need a Meshery deployment of your own.

What you will learn 🔗

  • How a design is built from components, relationships, and configuration, and how Kanvas saves it.
  • How Kanvas checks a design before it touches a cluster.
  • How a design becomes running resources, and how Kanvas tracks them afterward.
  • Which capabilities work on hosted Kanvas and which need a Meshery you run.

The model in four steps 🔗

  1. Design. In Designer mode you describe infrastructure as a design: components (such as a Kubernetes Deployment or Service), the relationships between them, and their configuration.
  2. Validate. Kanvas checks the design against each component’s schema and attaches every error to the component and field that caused it; a dry run then checks the design against a real cluster without changing it.
  3. Deploy. Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes clusters you select and labels every resource it creates with the design’s identity.
  4. Operate. In Operator mode you see the live state of your clusters and can filter it to the resources that belong to one design.

Where do you want to work? 🔗

Kanvas runs in two places. Both use the same Designer, but only a Meshery you run can reach your clusters.

item.title: Canvas Actions
item.description:
Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the Canvas Actions menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.

The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.

item.title: Layout and Layers
item.description:
Two controls decide how a design reads on screen. Layout arranges the components - where they sit relative to one another. Layers decide which of them are drawn at all.

Both are recorded in the design rather than in your browser, so they travel with it: a layout writes the components’ positions, and the Layers panel writes their visibility into the design’s preferences. Anyone else opening the design sees the same arrangement and the same components hidden. What neither touches is configuration - a hidden component is still part of the design and is still deployed, and re-running a layout changes only where components sit.

item.title: Merging and Loading Designs
item.description:
Designs are rarely built from nothing. A platform design usually starts from an existing one - a team’s base cluster layout, a reference architecture from the catalog, a design a colleague already published - which you then extend. Kanvas supports that by letting you drag a design straight onto the canvas and decide, at that moment, whether it should join what is already there or replace it.

Dragging a design onto the canvas 🔗

Drag a design from the design list, the catalog or your workspace and drop it onto the canvas.

item.title: Saving Designs
item.description:
While you are signed in, Kanvas saves for you. There is no save button you must remember to press before closing the tab: every change you make to a design - adding a component, moving it, editing its configuration, drawing a relationship, renaming the design - is persisted to your account as you make it.

That leaves two things worth knowing: how to tell whether a change has actually landed, and how to deliberately create a second, separate copy.

item.title: Create Relationships
item.description:
Relationships record how components connect, and Kanvas keeps related configuration in sync once they exist. You create some relationships by hand and Kanvas creates others when it evaluates the design. This guide shows which is which, how to create each kind, and how to remove or hide them.

Relationships work only in Designer mode. For what each kind means, read Relationships.

Kind You create it by You remove it by
Edge (network, mount, reference, and other edge subtypes) Picking an edge from a component’s handle and dragging to a target Selecting the edge and choosing Delete
Hierarchical, inventory Dropping a component onto a compatible parent Dragging it out, or choosing Move Out of Parent
Hierarchical, wallet Dropping a component onto a compatible host Deleting the component, or choosing Move Out of Parent
Hierarchical, alias Kanvas creates it during evaluation Deleting the alias component
TagSets (shared labels) Giving components matching labels Changing the labels so they stop matching
Annotation edge Drawing with the Pen tool Selecting the edge and choosing Delete

Create an edge relationship 🔗

Edge relationships connect components that exchange traffic or depend on one another, such as a Service and a Deployment.

item.title: Deploy and Observe Your First Design
item.description:
In this tutorial you take the design you saved in Create Your First Design to a live Kubernetes cluster. You validate it, dry-run it against the cluster, deploy it, and then switch to Operator mode to see the running resources that belong to the design. You finish by undeploying it.

Along the way you learn the difference between checking a design against its schemas and checking it against a cluster, how Kanvas chooses where to deploy, and how Kanvas keeps track of the resources a design creates.

item.title: Relationships
item.description: A relationship records how two components connect: one runs inside the other, one sends traffic to the other, one mounts the other’s storage, or both carry the same label. Relationships do more than draw lines. Each relationship definition names the configuration fields on both sides that must agree, so Kanvas can write values from one component into the other and keep the design consistent as you edit. The definitions come from the Meshery registry, not from Kanvas, so the set of relationships available to you depends on the models you use.

item.title: Policy Evaluation
item.description: Evaluation is how a design stays consistent. After you change a design, Kanvas runs it through the policy engine, which applies the registry’s relationship definitions: it identifies relationships, writes configuration across related components, and drops relationships that no longer hold. The engine returns the whole evaluated design, and Kanvas applies it back to the canvas. This is why a value you did not touch can change a moment after you edit a related component.

item.title: Whiteboard on the Canvas
item.description:
Whiteboarding in Kanvas (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.

Whiteboarding lets you diagram freely on the same canvas as your infrastructure. You draw shapes, text, freehand strokes, and lines to explain intent, and they sit beside real components in one design. It is on by default and available on every plan.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
Kanvas rests on one idea: a design is a declarative description of infrastructure. It records which components exist, how they relate to each other, how each one is configured, and any annotations that explain the intent. A design describes the state you want; it is not a script of steps to run.

Each part of Kanvas plays one role around that design:

  • Designer authors the design. You place components, connect them, and configure them on a shared canvas. Every save creates a new version, and collaborators can edit the same design at the same time.
  • Meshery validates and deploys the design. It checks the design against component schemas, dry-runs it against target clusters, and deploys or undeploys it on the Kubernetes contexts you choose.
  • Operator shows the running result. It displays live cluster state and links it back to the design: every resource Kanvas deploys carries the identity of its source design, so Operator can show exactly what one design produced.

Layer5 Cloud, as the remote provider, stores designs and their versions and governs who can see them. Every new design starts public; Designs and Components explains visibility in full.

item.title: Work with Tags
item.description:
Tags are the key-value labels and annotations on a component. When components share matching labels, Kanvas groups them in a TagSet, a shaded region drawn around the matching components. Use tags to see which components belong together, such as the Service and Deployment of one application.

item.title: Publishing Designs
item.description: Publishing a design lets you make your content visible to any anonymous visitor of https://cloud.layer5.io/catalog and any Layer5 Cloud user. Anyone with the link can view the design. You can publish the design into your Cloud Catalog.
